bodyHtml: Erasure is only one right; users can also request a copy of all their data; you need a way to export JOIN across all tables for a given userId

lessonTitle: Backup Strategy — RTO, RPO, Real Restore Testing
lead: Storing backups in the same location as the database
bodyHtml: If the server dies, the backups die with it; always store backups off-site (S3, different region)

lessonTitle: Backup Strategy — RTO, RPO, Real Restore Testing
lead: Never testing restores
bodyHtml: A backup that has never been restored is not a backup; schedule monthly restore tests and treat test failures as incidents

lessonTitle: Backup Strategy — RTO, RPO, Real Restore Testing
lead: Backing up only the system database
bodyHtml: Your per-tenant databases contain your customers' data; each tenant database needs its own backup schedule

lessonTitle: Backup Strategy — RTO, RPO, Real Restore Testing
lead: Not accounting for Redis
bodyHtml: Your Redis session hashes are important; if Redis loses data (restart without persistence), active sessions are invalidated; enable Redis AOF persistence or accept the tradeoff explicitly

lessonTitle: Multi-Tenant Data Isolation Models
lead: Missing `tenantId` checks in service methods
bodyHtml: In database-per-tenant, the database boundary enforces isolation; if you ever add shared-schema features, you must add explicit WHERE tenantId = $1 guards or the ORM-level scope

lessonTitle: Multi-Tenant Data Isolation Models
lead: Connection pool explosion
bodyHtml: Naive implementation: every request creates a new DataSource; correct: LRU cache with bounded pool sizes; you likely have this, but verify the eviction policy

lessonTitle: Multi-Tenant Data Isolation Models
lead: Running tenant migrations without verification
bodyHtml: A migration that fails on tenant 50 of 200 leaves the remaining 150 on the old schema; implement the migration runner from item 43 with retry and idempotency

lessonTitle: Multi-Tenant Data Isolation Models
lead: No tenant offboarding process
bodyHtml: Every provisioned database costs money; implement deprovisioning for churned tenants and test that it correctly drops the database and revokes credentials

lessonTitle: Event Log Rehydration (Rebuilding State from Event Log)
lead: Mutating events retroactively
bodyHtml: events are facts. Never update an existing event row. Append a corrective event instead (EmailCorrected).

lessonTitle: Event Log Rehydration (Rebuilding State from Event Log)
lead: Skipping version gaps
bodyHtml: if you allow out-of-order appends without a version check, you get corrupt state. Always enforce a WHERE version = $expectedNextVersion constraint on insert.

lessonTitle: Event Log Rehydration (Rebuilding State from Event Log)
lead: Not snapshotting
bodyHtml: an aggregate with 10,000 events is slow to rehydrate on every request. Cache a snapshot every N events and replay only the tail.

lessonTitle: Event Log Rehydration (Rebuilding State from Event Log)
lead: Fat events with derived data
bodyHtml: store only the minimal facts in the event payload. Computed fields belong in the projection, not the event itself.

lessonTitle: OLTP vs OLAP — Analytical vs Transactional Workload Separation
lead: Running unbounded aggregations in API handlers
bodyHtml: COUNT(*) FROM audit_log WHERE tenant_id = ? will eventually bring your app to its knees as the table grows.

lessonTitle: OLTP vs OLAP — Analytical vs Transactional Workload Separation
lead: Ignoring read replicas
bodyHtml: if your cloud provider (e.g., RDS, Supabase, Neon) offers read replicas, use them for all reporting queries — free performance headroom.

lessonTitle: OLTP vs OLAP — Analytical vs Transactional Workload Separation
lead: Over-engineering early
bodyHtml: you do not need Snowflake at 100 tenants. Start with materialized views and a BullMQ refresh job; migrate to a warehouse when the pain is real.

lessonTitle: OLTP vs OLAP — Analytical vs Transactional Workload Separation
lead: Forgetting to index analytical queries
bodyHtml: even on a read replica, an unindexed GROUP BY on a 10M-row table takes minutes; add composite indexes or partial indexes for common analytical filters.

lessonTitle: N+1 Query Problem
lead: Fixing N+1 with `Promise.all` (parallel N queries)
bodyHtml: Promise.all(items.map(id => db.user.findUnique(...))) still fires N queries in parallel — faster than sequential, but still N queries; use include or batch with findMany({ where: { id: { in: ids } } }) instead

lessonTitle: N+1 Query Problem
lead: Over-including relations
bodyHtml: Fixing N+1 by include-ing everything results in huge payloads and slow JOIN-heavy queries; select only the fields and relations the endpoint actually uses

lessonTitle: N+1 Query Problem
lead: No query logging in development
bodyHtml: Without Prisma's query logging or a tool like Prisma Studio, N+1 problems are invisible; add log: ['query'] to your dev PrismaClient to see every query

lessonTitle: N+1 Query Problem
lead: Assuming Prisma's `include` uses JOINs
bodyHtml: Prisma uses a batched second query, not a JOIN, for relations; this means two queries, not N+1 — but for very large datasets, a raw SQL JOIN might be more efficient

lessonTitle: Database Index Strategy (Composite, Covering, Partial Index)
lead: Over-indexing
bodyHtml: Every index slows down writes; tables with 8 indexes on 10 columns are common in over-indexed apps; index based on actual query plans, not hypothetical ones

lessonTitle: Database Index Strategy (Composite, Covering, Partial Index)
lead: Wrong composite column order
bodyHtml: An index on (status, tenant_id) won't help a query that only filters on tenant_id; put the column appearing in the most standalone WHERE clauses first

lessonTitle: Database Index Strategy (Composite, Covering, Partial Index)
lead: Partial indexes with functions
bodyHtml: WHERE expires_at > NOW() creates a partial index with a snapshot condition at creation time — it doesn't dynamically filter; for time-based partial indexes, use explicit cutoff columns or accept the index covers the full table

lessonTitle: Database Index Strategy (Composite, Covering, Partial Index)
lead: Not using `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY`
bodyHtml: Creating an index without CONCURRENTLY takes a write lock on the table, blocking all writes for the duration; always use CONCURRENTLY for indexes on production tables

lessonTitle: Query Plan Analysis — EXPLAIN ANALYZE
lead: Running `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` on a write query in production
bodyHtml: ANALYZE executes the query — an ANALYZE on a DELETE or UPDATE runs it for real; use EXPLAIN (without ANALYZE) for writes, or wrap in a transaction you immediately roll back

lessonTitle: Query Plan Analysis — EXPLAIN ANALYZE
lead: Ignoring the row estimate vs actual row discrepancy
bodyHtml: A plan that looks efficient based on estimates can be catastrophic when estimates are 100x off; check "rows=N" vs "actual rows=N" and run VACUUM ANALYZE table if they diverge significantly

lessonTitle: Query Plan Analysis — EXPLAIN ANALYZE
lead: Assuming adding an index will always help
bodyHtml: PostgreSQL uses the index only if the planner estimates it's cheaper; for queries returning more than ~5–10% of the table, a seq scan is faster; don't add an index and assume it's being used — verify with EXPLAIN

lessonTitle: Query Plan Analysis — EXPLAIN ANALYZE
lead: Not using `EXPLAIN (FORMAT JSON)`
bodyHtml: The JSON format (EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, FORMAT JSON)) can be pasted into tools like explain.dalibo.com for a visual plan; much easier to read for complex multi-join queries

lessonTitle: Connection Pool Tuning (pgBouncer, HikariCP)
lead: Creating a new PrismaClient on every request
bodyHtml: In Next.js, if you instantiate new PrismaClient() at the module level without the singleton pattern, each hot-reload in dev creates a new pool and exhausts connections

lessonTitle: Connection Pool Tuning (pgBouncer, HikariCP)
lead: Using pgBouncer transaction mode with session-level features
bodyHtml: Advisory locks (pg_advisory_lock), prepared statements, and SET variables require session mode or direct connections; using them in transaction mode causes silent misbehavior

lessonTitle: Connection Pool Tuning (pgBouncer, HikariCP)
lead: Not adding `?pgbouncer=true` to the connection string
bodyHtml: Without this flag, Prisma uses named prepared statements that pgBouncer can't multiplex correctly in transaction mode; always add this flag when using pgBouncer

lessonTitle: Connection Pool Tuning (pgBouncer, HikariCP)
lead: Setting `connection_limit` too high on serverless
bodyHtml: A Vercel app with 200 concurrent functions and connection_limit=10 presents 2,000 connections to pgBouncer or directly to PostgreSQL; use connection_limit=1 or 2 on serverless and let the pooler do the multiplexing

lessonTitle: Redis Cache Strategies (Write-Through, Write-Behind, Cache-Aside)
lead: Caching mutable objects without invalidation
bodyHtml: A cached tenant config that is never invalidated will serve stale data indefinitely after an admin changes a setting; every write path must also update or invalidate the relevant cache keys

lessonTitle: Redis Cache Strategies (Write-Through, Write-Behind, Cache-Aside)
lead: Using a global cache key (no tenant scoping)
bodyHtml: cache:users instead of cache:users:${tenantId} — in a multi-tenant SaaS, cross-tenant data leakage via shared cache keys is a serious security issue

lessonTitle: Redis Cache Strategies (Write-Through, Write-Behind, Cache-Aside)
lead: Not handling Redis unavailability in cache-aside
bodyHtml: If Redis is down and your cache-aside falls back to the DB, that's correct behavior — but make sure the fallback path exists and is tested; don't let Redis downtime cause 500s

lessonTitle: Redis Cache Strategies (Write-Through, Write-Behind, Cache-Aside)
lead: Write-behind for financial data
bodyHtml: If Redis crashes between a write-behind and the DB flush, you've lost the data permanently; write-behind is only for ephemeral, loss-tolerant data

lessonTitle: CDN Cache Strategy — Cache-Control, stale-while-revalidate
lead: No `Cache-Control` header = platform default caching
bodyHtml: Some CDNs (Cloudflare) cache responses with no Cache-Control header by default; an absent header is not the same as "no cache"

lessonTitle: CDN Cache Strategy — Cache-Control, stale-while-revalidate
lead: Caching tenant-specific responses as `public`
bodyHtml: If Cloudflare or Vercel's edge caches a tenant dashboard under a shared URL, the next user to request that URL gets the first tenant's data — a security incident

lessonTitle: CDN Cache Strategy — Cache-Control, stale-while-revalidate
lead: Using `Vary: Cookie`
bodyHtml: This prevents CDN caching for any request with a cookie, which is every authenticated request; instead of Vary: Cookie, use private for authenticated responses and restrict CDN caching to public routes

lessonTitle: CDN Cache Strategy — Cache-Control, stale-while-revalidate
lead: Misunderstanding `no-cache` vs `no-store`
bodyHtml: no-cache means "you may cache it, but revalidate with the origin on every use" — it's not the same as disabling caching; use no-store when you genuinely don't want any caching

lessonTitle: CAP Theorem
lead: Treating the whole system as one CAP choice
bodyHtml: Your PostgreSQL, Redis, and any future message broker each have their own CP/AP tradeoff — document them separately

lessonTitle: CAP Theorem
lead: Ignoring partition tolerance entirely
bodyHtml: "Our database is always up" is not a partition tolerance strategy; networks fail, containers restart, and cloud AZs go down

lessonTitle: CAP Theorem
lead: Confusing consistency levels
bodyHtml: PostgreSQL READ COMMITTED (the default) is not strongly consistent — dirty reads are prevented, but you can still read different values in the same transaction under certain isolation levels

lessonTitle: CAP Theorem
lead: Not considering PACELC
bodyHtml: Even without partitions, read replicas and caches trade consistency for latency — acknowledge this in your architecture, especially for features like billing or entitlement checks

lessonTitle: Event Sourcing + CQRS
lead: Using it everywhere
bodyHtml: Event sourcing is heavyweight; a UserPreferences CRUD table does not need an event log

lessonTitle: Event Sourcing + CQRS
lead: Mutable events
bodyHtml: Events must be immutable and versioned; never UPDATE an event row — only append new corrective events

lessonTitle: Event Sourcing + CQRS
lead: Forgetting snapshots
bodyHtml: Replaying 50,000 events on every aggregate load is a performance disaster; add snapshots once event counts grow

lessonTitle: Event Sourcing + CQRS
lead: Tight coupling between event producer and projection
bodyHtml: Projections should be independently deployable consumers; if the projection logic lives in the same transaction as the event write, you've defeated the purpose

lessonTitle: Circuit Breaker, Bulkhead, Retry
lead: Retrying non-idempotent operations
bodyHtml: A payment charge retried three times without an idempotency key results in three charges; always pass idempotency keys to external APIs before adding retries

lessonTitle: Circuit Breaker, Bulkhead, Retry
lead: No jitter
bodyHtml: Exponential backoff without jitter causes synchronized retry storms — every client backs off to the same interval and fires simultaneously when it expires

lessonTitle: Circuit Breaker, Bulkhead, Retry
lead: One circuit breaker for all services
bodyHtml: A single global circuit breaker that trips on Stripe failures also blocks email sends; isolate by dependency

lessonTitle: Circuit Breaker, Bulkhead, Retry
lead: Catching and silencing circuit open errors
bodyHtml: If the circuit is open, you should either serve a degraded response (e.g., show cached data) or surface a clear error — not catch and return null, which hides the failure

lessonTitle: Rate Limiting Strategies (Token Bucket, Leaky Bucket, Sliding Window)
lead: Not returning rate limit headers
bodyHtml: Clients that don't know their limit or remaining count will retry aggressively; always send X-RateLimit-* headers with every response

lessonTitle: Rate Limiting Strategies (Token Bucket, Leaky Bucket, Sliding Window)
lead: Limiting by IP on load-balanced endpoints
bodyHtml: Users behind NAT or corporate proxies share IPs; limit by authenticated identity whenever possible, fall back to IP only for unauthenticated routes

lessonTitle: Rate Limiting Strategies (Token Bucket, Leaky Bucket, Sliding Window)
lead: Non-atomic Redis operations
bodyHtml: GET then SET is a race condition; use Lua scripts or Redis transactions (MULTI/EXEC) for all counter operations

lessonTitle: Rate Limiting Strategies (Token Bucket, Leaky Bucket, Sliding Window)
lead: Same limit for all tenants
bodyHtml: A free-tier tenant and a high-volume enterprise tenant should not share the same rate limit; make limits configurable per plan in your tenant settings

lessonTitle: Distributed Locking (Redis Redlock, DB-based)
lead: Not using a TTL on Redis locks
bodyHtml: A process that crashes while holding the lock will deadlock all other processes indefinitely until the key is manually deleted

lessonTitle: Distributed Locking (Redis Redlock, DB-based)
lead: Releasing someone else's lock
bodyHtml: Always use the check-and-delete Lua script; a plain DEL key will release a lock that another process re-acquired after your TTL expired

lessonTitle: Distributed Locking (Redis Redlock, DB-based)
lead: Setting TTL too short
bodyHtml: If the critical section takes longer than the TTL, the lock expires while you're still in it; another process acquires the lock and you have two holders — set TTL to 3–5x the expected operation duration

lessonTitle: Distributed Locking (Redis Redlock, DB-based)
lead: Using Redlock for very short operations
bodyHtml: For operations entirely within a PostgreSQL transaction, pg_advisory_xact_lock is simpler, safer (ACID), and has no TTL management — prefer it over Redis locks for DB-scoped critical sections

lessonTitle: Webhook Security & Retry Mechanism
lead: Verifying the JSON-parsed body instead of the raw body
bodyHtml: JSON parsing is not deterministic — key ordering or whitespace differences change the hash; always verify against the raw bytes before parsing

lessonTitle: Webhook Security & Retry Mechanism
lead: Using `===` for signature comparison
bodyHtml: Regular string comparison leaks timing information; always use crypto.timingSafeEqual()

lessonTitle: Webhook Security & Retry Mechanism
lead: No timestamp window
bodyHtml: A valid signed request from yesterday can be replayed indefinitely without a timestamp check

lessonTitle: Webhook Security & Retry Mechanism
lead: Exposing webhook endpoints without rate limiting
bodyHtml: Even with signature verification, an attacker can generate valid signatures with their own test keys; rate limit webhook endpoints by IP to prevent resource exhaustion

lessonTitle: API Versioning Strategies (URL vs Header vs Content Negotiation)
lead: Adding versioning only after the first breaking change
bodyHtml: By then you already have clients on the "v0" implicit version; you have to version-bump everything retroactively and it's a mess

lessonTitle: API Versioning Strategies (URL vs Header vs Content Negotiation)
lead: Maintaining separate full codebases per version
bodyHtml: Version-specific logic should be at the serialization/transformation layer, not duplicated business logic — one source of truth, multiple output shapes

lessonTitle: API Versioning Strategies (URL vs Header vs Content Negotiation)
lead: No sunset dates
bodyHtml: A v1 that was supposed to die in January 2024 is still running in 2026 because no one set a deadline and communicated it to clients

lessonTitle: API Versioning Strategies (URL vs Header vs Content Negotiation)
lead: Versioning every endpoint separately
bodyHtml: If you have /api/v1/users and /api/v2/users but /api/v1/tenants never got updated, the version signal is meaningless — version the API as a whole, not per-resource

lessonTitle: Backward/Forward Compatibility — Schema Evolution
lead: `NOT NULL` without `DEFAULT` on an existing table
bodyHtml: PostgreSQL must validate every existing row at migration time — this locks the table; always provide a DEFAULT or backfill first

lessonTitle: Backward/Forward Compatibility — Schema Evolution
lead: Removing fields in the same migration that adds replacements
bodyHtml: The expand step (add new) and the contract step (remove old) must be separate deployments with at least one full deploy cycle in between

lessonTitle: Backward/Forward Compatibility — Schema Evolution
lead: `.strict()` on Zod schemas for incoming event/message data
bodyHtml: Makes your consumer brittle against any new field the producer adds; remove .strict() from external message schemas

lessonTitle: Backward/Forward Compatibility — Schema Evolution
lead: Assuming migrations are instantaneous
bodyHtml: Long-running migrations (backfills on large tables) hold locks; use pg_repack or batched background updates for tables with millions of rows

lessonTitle: Read Replica Routing in Prisma/TypeORM
lead: Reading from replica immediately after a write in the same request
bodyHtml: The replica may be 50–200ms behind; always use .$primary() for reads that must reflect a just-completed write (e.g., return the updated record after saving it)

lessonTitle: Read Replica Routing in Prisma/TypeORM
lead: Running transactions on the replica connection
bodyHtml: Transactions that contain writes must go to the primary; some drivers silently route them correctly, others don't — always verify

lessonTitle: Read Replica Routing in Prisma/TypeORM
lead: Not monitoring replication lag
bodyHtml: Unmonitored replication lag can grow silently during write bursts; set up a pg_stat_replication check or a CloudWatch/Datadog metric with an alert threshold

lessonTitle: Read Replica Routing in Prisma/TypeORM
lead: Assuming one pool is enough
bodyHtml: The replica connection pool must be sized independently from the primary pool; read traffic patterns differ significantly from write traffic

lessonTitle: Database Sharding Strategies
lead: Sharding prematurely
bodyHtml: Most SaaS applications at $1M ARR don't need sharding; PostgreSQL with proper indexing and a read replica handles enormous scale; sharding adds enormous operational complexity for a problem you likely don't have

lessonTitle: Database Sharding Strategies
lead: Using a timestamp as the shard key
bodyHtml: All inserts go to the "latest" shard, which becomes a hotspot while all other shards are idle

lessonTitle: Database Sharding Strategies
lead: Forgetting about cross-shard JOINs
bodyHtml: If you shard users and they have foreign keys to other tables in a different shard, you've lost referential integrity — this must be handled in application code

lessonTitle: Database Sharding Strategies
lead: Conflating sharding with partitioning
bodyHtml: PostgreSQL table partitioning (PARTITION BY RANGE) splits one logical table into multiple physical storage files within a single database instance — much simpler than sharding, and often sufficient for large append-only tables

lessonTitle: CQRS Read Model Optimization (Materialized Views)
lead: Refreshing without `CONCURRENTLY`
bodyHtml: A plain REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW takes an exclusive lock and blocks all reads on that view for the duration — always use CONCURRENTLY in production (requires a unique index)

lessonTitle: CQRS Read Model Optimization (Materialized Views)
lead: Forgetting to refresh
bodyHtml: A materialized view that never gets refreshed is just a stale table; wire up the refresh to BullMQ or a cron job and monitor its last-refresh timestamp

lessonTitle: CQRS Read Model Optimization (Materialized Views)
lead: Denormalizing everything eagerly
bodyHtml: Not every table needs a read model; profile first, then denormalize the specific queries that are slow — premature denormalization creates synchronization bugs

lessonTitle: CQRS Read Model Optimization (Materialized Views)
lead: Not handling consistency between write model and read model
bodyHtml: If you maintain a denormalized column (like memberCount) but forget to update it in one code path, it drifts silently — use database transactions to update both atomically, or use PostgreSQL triggers as a safety net

lessonTitle: Outbox Pattern
lead: Polling without `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`
bodyHtml: Multiple relay instances polling without this will pick the same rows, resulting in duplicate publishes; SKIP LOCKED ensures each relay instance works on a distinct subset

lessonTitle: Outbox Pattern
lead: Using Redis as the outbox store
bodyHtml: If Redis loses data before the relay publishes, you've lost the message; the outbox must be in the same ACID database as your state

lessonTitle: Outbox Pattern
lead: Not cleaning up published messages
bodyHtml: The outbox table grows indefinitely; add a scheduled job to delete status = 'published' messages older than your retention window (e.g., 7 days)

lessonTitle: Outbox Pattern
lead: Publishing outside the transaction "for performance"
bodyHtml: The entire point of the outbox is atomic write-and-enqueue; moving the outboxMessage.create() outside the transaction defeats the pattern entirely

lessonTitle: Two-Phase Commit vs Eventual Consistency
lead: Assuming eventual consistency means "probably consistent"
bodyHtml: Eventual consistency is a guarantee of convergence, not "might or might not converge"; it requires correct implementation — idempotency, outbox, saga

lessonTitle: Two-Phase Commit vs Eventual Consistency
lead: Using 2PC in cloud/serverless environments
bodyHtml: Cloud databases (RDS, Aurora, PlanetScale, Supabase) often don't support PREPARE TRANSACTION or have it disabled; check before designing around it

lessonTitle: Two-Phase Commit vs Eventual Consistency
lead: Leaving "provisioning" status entities unmonitored
bodyHtml: Eventual consistency leaves entities in intermediate states; you need a monitor that alerts on entities stuck in status = 'provisioning' for more than N minutes

lessonTitle: Two-Phase Commit vs Eventual Consistency
lead: Not documenting the consistency model
bodyHtml: Saying "we use eventual consistency" without specifying the convergence mechanism and the maximum lag window leaves the next developer (you in 6 months) guessing

lessonTitle: Message Queues 101 — Pub/Sub and Point-to-Point Basics
lead: Using a queue as a database
bodyHtml: querying/filtering message backlogs instead of writing consumed data to a proper store

lessonTitle: Microservices vs Monolith — Service Boundary Design
lead: Adopting microservices before product-market fit, when the domain model itself is still changing weekly
bodyHtml: service boundaries drawn too early get redrawn constantly, at much higher cost than in a monolith

lessonTitle: Microservices vs Monolith — Service Boundary Design
lead: Underestimating the operational overhead
bodyHtml: each new service needs its own CI/CD, logging, tracing, alerting; this cost is real and ongoing, not a one-time setup tax

lessonTitle: Microservices vs Monolith — Service Boundary Design
lead: Treating the split as purely technical, without also splitting team ownership
bodyHtml: a shared team maintaining "microservices" gets none of the isolation benefit and all of the coordination cost

lessonTitle: Express: Two-Layer Architecture — Routes and Static Services
lead: Putting business logic in the route handler
bodyHtml: conditionals that decide pricing, permissions, or state transitions belong in the service, not sandwiched between safeParse and res.json.

lessonTitle: Express: Two-Layer Architecture — Routes and Static Services
lead: Importing Express types into a service
bodyHtml: a service that imports Request/Response has leaked an HTTP concern into business logic, making it untestable without mocking Express.

lessonTitle: Express: Two-Layer Architecture — Routes and Static Services
lead: **Reaching for `router.use("*", ...)`**
bodyHtml: this throws in Express 5; use router.use(fn) for "all paths in this router" instead.

lessonTitle: Express: Two-Layer Architecture — Routes and Static Services
lead: Scattering a module's files by technical type
bodyHtml: (routes/project.ts, services/project.ts in separate top-level folders) instead of colocating them under modules/project/ — this makes a single feature change touch four unrelated directories.

lessonTitle: Express: Middleware Pipeline, CORS, and Rate Limiting
lead: Registering the error handler before other middleware
bodyHtml: Express treats a 4-argument function anywhere in the stack as an error handler; putting it early means later middleware errors never reach it.

lessonTitle: Express: Middleware Pipeline, CORS, and Rate Limiting
lead: **Setting `origin: "*"` alongside `credentials: true`**
bodyHtml: this combination is invalid per the CORS spec and browsers will reject the response even though the server sends it.

lessonTitle: Express: Middleware Pipeline, CORS, and Rate Limiting
lead: Applying `apiLimiter` uniformly to login endpoints
bodyHtml: 100 requests per 15 minutes is far too permissive for a brute-forceable auth endpoint; those need authLimiter's tighter 10/15min ceiling.

lessonTitle: Express: Middleware Pipeline, CORS, and Rate Limiting
lead: Raising the global body size limit to accommodate one upload route
bodyHtml: override the limit locally on the specific route (or use multer) instead of loosening express.json() globally to 10mb+.

lessonTitle: Express: Curried Auth Middleware and Typed Request Augmentation
lead: Reading `req.user` without the middleware in the pipeline
bodyHtml: if a route reads req.user!.userId but never applied authMiddleware("USER"|"ADMIN"), it will crash at runtime despite compiling fine, because the non-null assertion lied to the compiler.

lessonTitle: Express: Curried Auth Middleware and Typed Request Augmentation
lead: Putting JWT verification logic inside the middleware itself
bodyHtml: this makes the crypto/Redis logic untestable without spinning up Express, and prevents reuse from non-HTTP entry points.

lessonTitle: Express: Curried Auth Middleware and Typed Request Augmentation
lead: Forgetting `authMiddleware("GUEST")` on public routes
bodyHtml: while it's a no-op, omitting it makes the route's auth posture ambiguous at a glance; every route should state its tier explicitly.

lessonTitle: Express: Curried Auth Middleware and Typed Request Augmentation
lead: Using `(req.user as SafeUser).userId` instead of `req.user!.userId`
bodyHtml: the as cast suppresses more type-checking than the non-null assertion and is inconsistent with the house convention.

lessonTitle: Express: Centralized Error Handling with AppError
lead: Building error responses inline in route handlers
bodyHtml: if (error instanceof AppError) return res.status(error.statusCode).json(...) inside every route duplicates errorHandler's job and guarantees the shape will drift over time.

lessonTitle: Express: Centralized Error Handling with AppError
lead: Registering `errorHandler` before other middleware or routers
bodyHtml: Express only routes an error to handlers registered after the point of failure; putting it first means it never fires.

lessonTitle: Express: Centralized Error Handling with AppError
lead: Double-logging an expected error
bodyHtml: calling Logger.error and then throwing AppError for the same not-found case creates noisy logs for something that isn't actually a problem; use Logger.warn for expected paths.

lessonTitle: Express: Centralized Error Handling with AppError
lead: Letting a non-critical failure crash the request
bodyHtml: a cache write or audit log wrapped in the outer try/catch (instead of its own local one) will turn a harmless side-effect failure into a 500 for the user.

lessonTitle: Express: Zod Validation and Response Envelope Conventions
lead: Validating query params without `z.coerce`
bodyHtml: page: z.number() will fail every request because req.query.page is the string "2", not the number 2; use z.coerce.number().

lessonTitle: Express: Zod Validation and Response Envelope Conventions
lead: Returning a naked array or a generic `{ data }` wrapper
bodyHtml: res.json(users) or res.json({ data: users }) breaks the entity-named-key convention that lets every response be typed consistently across the API.

lessonTitle: Express: Zod Validation and Response Envelope Conventions
lead: Re-validating input inside the service
bodyHtml: if the route already ran safeParse, a service that also checks if (!data.email) throw ... is duplicating a job that's already done, and risks the two validations drifting apart.

lessonTitle: Express: Zod Validation and Response Envelope Conventions
lead: Using `.parse()` on request bodies
bodyHtml: an uncaught throw from body validation skips the field-level ZodIssue[] response the frontend expects; bodies should use safeParse and build the 400 inline.

lessonTitle: Express: Real-Time Updates with SSE and Socket.io
lead: Reaching for Socket.io when SSE would do
bodyHtml: a notification stream or progress bar doesn't need a WebSocket; adding Socket.io's connection lifecycle and sticky-session requirement for a one-directional feature is unjustified complexity.

lessonTitle: Express: Real-Time Updates with SSE and Socket.io
lead: Broadcasting with `io.emit()`
bodyHtml: this sends the event to every connected client across every tenant and user; always scope to a room (user:{id}, tenant:{id}) instead.

lessonTitle: Express: Real-Time Updates with SSE and Socket.io
lead: Forgetting `res.flushHeaders()` on an SSE route
bodyHtml: without it, some reverse proxies buffer the entire response and the client sees nothing until the connection eventually closes, defeating the purpose of a live stream.

lessonTitle: Express: Real-Time Updates with SSE and Socket.io
lead: Authenticating Socket.io per-message instead of at the handshake
bodyHtml: checking the token inside every socket.on("event", ...) handler is redundant and slower; validate once in io.use() and trust socket.data.user afterward.

lessonTitle: Express: Integration Testing with Jest and Supertest
lead: Mocking the TypeORM repository
bodyHtml: a test that stubs userRepository.findOne to return a canned object proves nothing about whether the real query, real indexes, or real constraints behave correctly; use the real test database.

lessonTitle: Express: Integration Testing with Jest and Supertest
lead: Injecting `req.user` directly instead of logging in

lessonTitle: Express: Integration Testing with Jest and Supertest
lead: Truncating whole tables in `afterEach`
bodyHtml: this breaks parallel test execution and can silently delete fixtures another test file depends on; delete only the rows this test created.

lessonTitle: Express: Integration Testing with Jest and Supertest
lead: Skipping the auth-error and validation-error cases
bodyHtml: testing only the happy path leaves the two most common real-world failure modes (bad input, missing token) completely unverified.

lessonTitle: Spring Boot: Three-Layer Architecture — Controller, Service, and Repository
lead: Copying the Express static-service pattern into Spring Boot
bodyHtml: a static method bypasses the Spring proxy entirely, silently breaking @Transactional, @PreAuthorize, and any other AOP-based annotation on it.

lessonTitle: Spring Boot: Three-Layer Architecture — Controller, Service, and Repository
lead: Returning `@Entity` objects from the controller
bodyHtml: this leaks internal fields (password hashes, deletedAt, foreign keys) and couples the wire format to the JPA schema; always map through a response record.

lessonTitle: Spring Boot: Three-Layer Architecture — Controller, Service, and Repository
lead: Putting `@Transactional` on the controller
bodyHtml: the transactional boundary belongs in the service; controllers only handle HTTP concerns (including setting cookies, which is an intentional exception).

lessonTitle: Spring Boot: Three-Layer Architecture — Controller, Service, and Repository
lead: Field injection (`@Autowired` on a field)
bodyHtml: use constructor injection via @RequiredArgsConstructor; field injection hides dependencies and breaks clean unit testing.

lessonTitle: Spring Boot: Three-Layer Architecture — Controller, Service, and Repository
lead: Writing raw `EntityManager` queries in a service
bodyHtml: reach for a derived query method or @Query on the repository interface first; raw EntityManager is reserved for genuinely complex dynamic queries in a custom repository implementation.

lessonTitle: Spring Boot: ResponseEntity and Standard Response Records
lead: Returning the entity directly
bodyHtml: (ResponseEntity.ok(userEntity)) — exposes internal fields like password hashes and foreign keys that were never meant to leave the service layer.

lessonTitle: Spring Boot: ResponseEntity and Standard Response Records
lead: `ResponseEntity.ok(null)`
bodyHtml: a 200 with a null body is ambiguous; use ResponseEntity.noContent().build() (204) when there is genuinely nothing to return.

lessonTitle: Spring Boot: ResponseEntity and Standard Response Records
lead: Wrapping every response in `{ "success": true, "data": ... }`
bodyHtml: the HTTP status code already communicates success/failure; this envelope is unnecessary nesting that every client then has to unwrap.

lessonTitle: Spring Boot: ResponseEntity and Standard Response Records
lead: Using `Map<String, Object>` instead of a record
bodyHtml: loses compile-time safety and IDE support; define a record even for a two-field response.

lessonTitle: Spring Boot: ResponseEntity and Standard Response Records
lead: Mapping logic scattered across services instead of centralized in the record's factory
bodyHtml: leads to two services producing slightly different shapes of the "same" response.

lessonTitle: Spring Boot: Bean Validation with @Valid, @Validated, and Custom Constraints
lead: Adding `BindingResult` as a controller parameter
bodyHtml: this stops Spring from throwing MethodArgumentNotValidException automatically, forcing a manual check that bypasses the shared @ControllerAdvice error path. Acceptable only in server-rendered form flows, never in a REST API.

lessonTitle: Spring Boot: Bean Validation with @Valid, @Validated, and Custom Constraints
lead: Forgetting `@Validated` at the class level
bodyHtml: a bare @NotNull UUID userId path-variable parameter is silently unvalidated without it; this is the most common "why isn't validation firing" bug.

lessonTitle: Spring Boot: Bean Validation with @Valid, @Validated, and Custom Constraints
lead: Manual null/blank checks in the service
bodyHtml: (if (request.email() == null) throw ...) — this duplicates what Bean Validation already guarantees ran before the method body executed; if a manual check feels necessary, the constraint annotation is missing from the DTO.

lessonTitle: Spring Boot: Bean Validation with @Valid, @Validated, and Custom Constraints
lead: Omitting explicit `message()` on constraints
bodyHtml: the framework default ("must not be blank") is not written for end users; always supply a message meant to be read by a human.

lessonTitle: Spring Boot: Bean Validation with @Valid, @Validated, and Custom Constraints
lead: Reaching for validation groups when the fields genuinely differ
bodyHtml: groups add complexity; if create and update request shapes have little in common, two separate records are clearer than one record split by groups.

lessonTitle: Spring Boot: Service Layer Beans and @Transactional Scoping
lead: Copying Express's static-class service pattern
bodyHtml: public static UserResponse getById(...) bypasses the Spring proxy entirely; @Transactional on a static method has no effect.

lessonTitle: Spring Boot: Service Layer Beans and @Transactional Scoping
lead: Self-invocation of `@Transactional` methods
bodyHtml: calling this.method() from within the same class silently skips the proxy; split the caller and callee into separate beans.

lessonTitle: Spring Boot: Service Layer Beans and @Transactional Scoping
lead: `@Transactional` on an orchestration method that only calls other transactional services
bodyHtml: this inflates the outer transaction's duration for no correctness benefit; omit it unless true cross-call atomicity is required.

lessonTitle: Spring Boot: Service Layer Beans and @Transactional Scoping
lead: Field injection with `@Autowired`
bodyHtml: hides the bean's real dependencies and makes plain (non-Spring) unit testing awkward; use @RequiredArgsConstructor instead.

lessonTitle: Spring Boot: Service Layer Beans and @Transactional Scoping
lead: Returning `Optional<T>` or `null` from a service method to signal "not found"
bodyHtml: throw AppException instead; Optional is acceptable only as a repository return type resolved via .orElseThrow() inside the service.

lessonTitle: Spring Boot: Security Filter Chain, CORS, and Rate Limiting
lead: **Wildcard CORS origin (`List.of("*")`)**
bodyHtml: this silently blocks allowCredentials(true), which breaks httpOnly-cookie-based auth entirely; always read the origin from an environment variable.

lessonTitle: Spring Boot: Security Filter Chain, CORS, and Rate Limiting
lead: Forgetting `SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS`
bodyHtml: without it, Spring may create an HttpSession per request, which is both wasted memory and inconsistent with a JWT-only auth model.

lessonTitle: Spring Boot: Security Filter Chain, CORS, and Rate Limiting
lead: Registering the JWT filter after `authorizeHttpRequests` evaluates
bodyHtml: filter order is enforced by addFilterBefore placement, not declaration order in the file; the JWT filter must run before Spring checks the SecurityContext.

lessonTitle: Spring Boot: Security Filter Chain, CORS, and Rate Limiting
lead: Disabling CSRF without the stateless-JWT + `SameSite` cookie justification
bodyHtml: CSRF protection matters for session-cookie-based auth; disabling it is only safe under the specific conditions documented here, not a default to copy into a session-based app.

lessonTitle: Spring Boot: Security Filter Chain, CORS, and Rate Limiting
lead: Hardcoding rate limit thresholds inline instead of as named constants
bodyHtml: makes the policy harder to audit and keep in sync with the Express/Next.js equivalents.

lessonTitle: Spring Boot: JWT Authentication with OncePerRequestFilter and @PreAuthorize
lead: Throwing an exception directly from the JWT filter on an invalid token
bodyHtml: the filter should fail silently (log at debug, don't set authentication) and let authorizeHttpRequests produce the 401; throwing from the filter produces an inconsistent, harder-to-control error response.

lessonTitle: Spring Boot: JWT Authentication with OncePerRequestFilter and @PreAuthorize
lead: Manually prepending `ROLE_` in a `@PreAuthorize` expression
bodyHtml: (hasRole('ROLE_ADMIN')) — hasRole() already strips and re-adds the prefix; the correct usage is hasRole('ADMIN').

lessonTitle: Spring Boot: JWT Authentication with OncePerRequestFilter and @PreAuthorize
lead: Reading the user from `SecurityContextHolder` manually inside a controller
bodyHtml: instead of injecting @AuthenticationPrincipal CurrentUserDetails — the injection is type-safe, testable, and consistent across the codebase.

lessonTitle: Spring Boot: JWT Authentication with OncePerRequestFilter and @PreAuthorize
lead: Forgetting `@EnableMethodSecurity`
bodyHtml: without it on the SecurityConfig class, every @PreAuthorize annotation is silently ignored, and the route becomes accessible to any authenticated user regardless of role.

lessonTitle: Spring Boot: JWT Authentication with OncePerRequestFilter and @PreAuthorize
lead: Putting business logic inside the JWT filter
bodyHtml: the filter's only job is authentication (verify token, populate context); role-based authorization decisions belong in @PreAuthorize or the service layer, not in filter code.

lessonTitle: Spring Boot: Centralized Error Handling with @ControllerAdvice
lead: Crafting an error `ResponseEntity` inline inside a controller
bodyHtml: bypasses the uniform shape and logging the @ControllerAdvice provides; every controller method should let exceptions propagate.

lessonTitle: Spring Boot: Centralized Error Handling with @ControllerAdvice
lead: Logging at `error` level for expected `AppException` cases
bodyHtml: "user not found" is a normal negative path; use log.warn without a stack trace in the service, and reserve log.error for the catch-all unexpected-exception handler.

lessonTitle: Spring Boot: Centralized Error Handling with @ControllerAdvice
lead: Leaking the real exception message in the 500 response
bodyHtml: the catch-all handler must return a generic "Internal server error" string to the client while logging the real detail server-side only.

lessonTitle: Spring Boot: Centralized Error Handling with @ControllerAdvice
lead: Missing a handler for `HttpMessageNotReadableException`
bodyHtml: without it, malformed JSON falls into the generic 500 handler, which misrepresents a client error (bad request) as a server error.

lessonTitle: Spring Boot: Centralized Error Handling with @ControllerAdvice
lead: Silently swallowing an exception in a non-critical catch block
bodyHtml: without logging — even a "safe to ignore" failure (cache write) should be logged at warn so it's visible if it becomes systemic.

lessonTitle: Spring Boot: Flyway Migrations and Zero-Downtime Schema Changes
lead: Setting `ddl-auto: update` "temporarily" in dev
bodyHtml: this lets the schema silently drift from what Flyway tracks, and the drift surfaces as a confusing failure the moment validate catches it in a shared environment.

lessonTitle: Spring Boot: Flyway Migrations and Zero-Downtime Schema Changes
lead: Editing a migration file that has already run somewhere
bodyHtml: Flyway's checksum validation will fail startup in every environment where the old checksum was recorded; always add a new migration instead.

lessonTitle: Spring Boot: Flyway Migrations and Zero-Downtime Schema Changes
lead: Adding a `NOT NULL` column with no default directly to a live table
bodyHtml: this either fails outright (existing rows violate the constraint) or requires a full-table rewrite/lock; use the nullable → backfill → constrain sequence.

lessonTitle: Spring Boot: Flyway Migrations and Zero-Downtime Schema Changes
lead: Renaming a column referenced by running code in one migration
bodyHtml: this breaks any instance still running the old code during a rolling deploy; add the new column, migrate reads/writes, then drop the old one in a later migration.

lessonTitle: Spring Boot: Flyway Migrations and Zero-Downtime Schema Changes
lead: Testing against H2 in-memory instead of the real database engine
bodyHtml: H2 doesn't support Postgres-specific types, functions, or constraints, and passing tests there can hide bugs that only appear against real Postgres.

lessonTitle: Spring Boot: Testing with MockMvc, @WebMvcTest, and TestContainers
lead: Using `@WithMockUser` inside a full `@SpringBootTest`
bodyHtml: this bypasses the real JWT filter, meaning the test no longer proves the auth pipeline actually works; reserve @WithMockUser for @WebMvcTest slices.

lessonTitle: Spring Boot: Testing with MockMvc, @WebMvcTest, and TestContainers
lead: Mocking the repository in a full integration test
bodyHtml: defeats the purpose of @SpringBootTest; if the repository needs mocking, the test should be a @WebMvcTest or a plain Mockito unit test instead.

lessonTitle: Spring Boot: Testing with MockMvc, @WebMvcTest, and TestContainers
lead: Testing against H2 in-memory
bodyHtml: misses Postgres-specific behavior (types, constraints, functions) that TestContainers' real Postgres instance would catch.

lessonTitle: Spring Boot: Testing with MockMvc, @WebMvcTest, and TestContainers
lead: Truncating shared tables in `@AfterEach`
bodyHtml: breaks other test classes running in parallel against the same TestContainers instance; delete only the specific rows this test created.

lessonTitle: Spring Boot: Testing with MockMvc, @WebMvcTest, and TestContainers
lead: Still using `@MockBean`/`@SpyBean` in new code
bodyHtml: both are deprecated as of Spring Boot 3.4 and removed in Spring Boot 4; use @MockitoBean going forward.

lessonTitle: React Native: File Organization and Banned Patterns for Expo Apps
lead: Reading `process.env.X` directly in a component or hook
bodyHtml: bypasses the Zod validation in libs/env.ts and loses type safety; every env value should flow through ENV.

lessonTitle: React Native: File Organization and Banned Patterns for Expo Apps
lead: Storing a JWT in `AsyncStorage`
bodyHtml: it's unencrypted and readable by anything with filesystem access on a rooted/jailbroken device; use SecureStore for any token.

lessonTitle: React Native: File Organization and Banned Patterns for Expo Apps
lead: Co-locating a hook inside `components/[Feature]/useFeature.ts`
bodyHtml: the convention here is hooks/ for all hooks, so a second screen that needs the same data doesn't have to guess where to import it from.

lessonTitle: React Native: File Organization and Banned Patterns for Expo Apps
lead: Calling `fetch()` directly in a screen
bodyHtml: skips the auth header injection and 401-refresh interceptor that axiosInstance provides, silently producing unauthenticated requests.

lessonTitle: React Native: File Organization and Banned Patterns for Expo Apps
lead: Shipping `app.json` instead of `app.config.ts`
bodyHtml: loses the ability to type-check config and compute values (like reading EAS_PROJECT_ID) at build time.

lessonTitle: React Native: Expo Router Navigation and Protected Routes
lead: Putting the auth check in every screen instead of the group layout
bodyHtml: duplicates the same useEffect/redirect logic across every screen and risks a screen that forgets to check, briefly rendering protected content.

lessonTitle: React Native: Expo Router Navigation and Protected Routes
lead: Using `router.push()` for a visible tappable link
bodyHtml: loses the deep-linking and accessibility semantics <Link> provides for free; reserve router.push() for post-async navigation.

lessonTitle: React Native: Expo Router Navigation and Protected Routes
lead: Using `router.push()` instead of `router.replace()` after login
bodyHtml: leaves a back-stack entry that lets the user swipe/back-button their way back to the login screen after successfully authenticating.

lessonTitle: React Native: Expo Router Navigation and Protected Routes
lead: Reading `route.params` directly
bodyHtml: Expo Router's typed useLocalSearchParams<T>() is the supported API; reaching into a raw route object bypasses type safety and can break across Expo Router versions.

lessonTitle: React Native: Expo Router Navigation and Protected Routes
lead: Manually configuring `NavigationContainer`
bodyHtml: Expo Router owns this; a hand-rolled NavigationContainer alongside it produces duplicate/conflicting navigation state.

lessonTitle: React Native: Zustand + MMKV State Management
lead: Storing `accessToken`/`refreshToken` in Zustand state, persisted or not
bodyHtml: even in-memory-only Zustand state is one bug away from ending up in a MMKV-backed persist config; keep tokens exclusively in SecureStore.

lessonTitle: React Native: Zustand + MMKV State Management
lead: Calling `useAuthStore()` with no selector
bodyHtml: subscribes the component to every field in the store, causing unrelated state changes elsewhere to trigger unnecessary re-renders.

lessonTitle: React Native: Zustand + MMKV State Management
lead: Using `AsyncStorage` as the Zustand persist backend
bodyHtml: its async API doesn't match Zustand's synchronous StateStorage interface well and is measurably slower than MMKV.

lessonTitle: React Native: Zustand + MMKV State Management
lead: Reaching for React Context for a new piece of global state
bodyHtml: Context is reserved for dependency injection (e.g. a test double); any state visible across unrelated screens belongs in a Zustand store.

lessonTitle: React Native: Zustand + MMKV State Management
lead: Building a custom toast queue in Zustand
bodyHtml: sonner-native already solves this; a hand-rolled store duplicates functionality and needs its own root-level renderer wiring.

lessonTitle: React Native: Data Fetching, Loading States, and Offline Detection
lead: Omitting the `cancelled` flag in a single-item fetch hook
bodyHtml: causes a "Can't perform a React state update on an unmounted component" warning (or worse, a stale overwrite) when the screen unmounts mid-request.

lessonTitle: React Native: Data Fetching, Loading States, and Offline Detection
lead: Reaching for `fetch()` or a new axios instance instead of the shared `axiosInstance`
bodyHtml: loses the auth header injection and 401-refresh interceptor every other request in the app relies on.

lessonTitle: React Native: Data Fetching, Loading States, and Offline Detection
lead: A mutation with only a toast and no haptic
bodyHtml: on a physical device, haptic feedback is what makes an action feel confirmed; a toast alone is easy to miss if the user has already looked away from the screen.

lessonTitle: React Native: Data Fetching, Loading States, and Offline Detection
lead: Duplicating offline-detection `NetInfo` listeners per screen
bodyHtml: wastes native listener overhead and risks each screen showing a slightly different offline UI; wire it once at the root and let a single banner reflect it everywhere.

lessonTitle: React Native: Data Fetching, Loading States, and Offline Detection
lead: Inline `err.response?.data?.message` access at each call site
bodyHtml: when the Axios error shape changes (a new API error envelope, for instance), every call site has to be found and updated instead of one shared helper.

lessonTitle: React Native: Expo Config, Permissions, and Native Device APIs
lead: Keeping `app.json` instead of migrating to `app.config.ts`
bodyHtml: loses type safety and the ability to compute values like the EAS project ID from an environment variable.

lessonTitle: React Native: Expo Config, Permissions, and Native Device APIs
lead: Calling a device API without checking the permission result first
bodyHtml: produces an inconsistent no-op on iOS and a hard crash on some Android versions instead of a clean, user-facing message.

lessonTitle: React Native: Expo Config, Permissions, and Native Device APIs

bodyHtml: the resulting token has no user to attach to, and simulators return null, so testing this path only in a simulator hides the bug entirely.

lessonTitle: React Native: Expo Config, Permissions, and Native Device APIs
lead: Skipping the Android notification channel setup
bodyHtml: notifications silently never appear on Android even though the exact same code works on iOS.

lessonTitle: React Native: Expo Config, Permissions, and Native Device APIs
lead: Calling haptics inside a `useEffect` with no user gesture
bodyHtml: a vibration with no visible cause reads as a bug, not a confirmation, and erodes trust in the rest of the app's feedback.

lessonTitle: React Native: Expo Config, Permissions, and Native Device APIs
lead: Editing `android/` or `ios/` directly in a managed Expo workflow
bodyHtml: the directories are gitignored and regenerated on the next prebuild, silently discarding the change.

lessonTitle: React Native: NativeWind Styling, Design Tokens, and Dark Mode

bodyHtml: breaks dark mode (raw palette classes don't have a dark: counterpart wired to the token system) and diverges from the web layer's color language.

lessonTitle: React Native: NativeWind Styling, Design Tokens, and Dark Mode

lessonTitle: React Native: NativeWind Styling, Design Tokens, and Dark Mode

lessonTitle: React Native: NativeWind Styling, Design Tokens, and Dark Mode
lead: Forgetting `key={columns}` on a `FlatList` with dynamic `numColumns`

lessonTitle: React Native: NativeWind Styling, Design Tokens, and Dark Mode

bodyHtml: it's meant for imperative side effects; useColorScheme() already re-renders the component tree on OS theme change, so a hand-rolled listener duplicates work and can drift out of sync.

lessonTitle: React Native: NativeWind Styling, Design Tokens, and Dark Mode
lead: A raw `View` at a screen's top level instead of `SafeAreaView`/`useSafeAreaInsets`
bodyHtml: content renders under the status bar or behind the home indicator on notched devices.

lessonTitle: React Native: Accessibility and Feedback Patterns

bodyHtml: VoiceOver/TalkBack announce nothing useful, and the control is effectively unusable for a screen-reader user even though it works visually.

lessonTitle: React Native: Accessibility and Feedback Patterns
lead: Forcing an `accessibilityRole` that has no real match

lessonTitle: React Native: Accessibility and Feedback Patterns

bodyHtml: a sighted user sees the confirmation; a screen-reader user gets nothing unless they happen to be focused on the toast region.

lessonTitle: React Native: Accessibility and Feedback Patterns
lead: Letting an error toast auto-dismiss on the same timer as success
bodyHtml: the user may not have finished reading the failure reason before it vanishes; error toasts stay until dismissed.

lessonTitle: React Native: Accessibility and Feedback Patterns
lead: Showing a spinner immediately with no delay threshold
bodyHtml: a sub-100ms response produces a visible flash that reads as jank rather than smoothness.

lessonTitle: React Native: Accessibility and Feedback Patterns
lead: Shrinking a touch target to match a small icon's visual size

lessonTitle: React Native: Testing with Jest, React Native Testing Library, and Maestro
lead: Mocking `axiosInstance` directly instead of intercepting with MSW
bodyHtml: the test no longer verifies the actual request/response shape, so a backend contract change can break production without breaking the test.

lessonTitle: React Native: Testing with Jest, React Native Testing Library, and Maestro
lead: Forgetting to reset a Zustand store's state in `afterEach`
bodyHtml: a test that sets isAuthenticated: true leaks into the next test file, producing failures that only appear depending on run order.

lessonTitle: React Native: Testing with Jest, React Native Testing Library, and Maestro
lead: Testing `router.push`'s exact call signature instead of the resulting screen
bodyHtml: couples the test to implementation details that can change without the user-visible behavior changing at all.

lessonTitle: React Native: Testing with Jest, React Native Testing Library, and Maestro
lead: Trying to E2E-test a full login-to-checkout flow with `@testing-library/react-native`
bodyHtml: component-level tools aren't built for cross-screen, permission-crossing flows; that's what Maestro is for.

lessonTitle: React Native: Testing with Jest, React Native Testing Library, and Maestro
lead: Skipping `jest.mock("react-native-mmkv")`
bodyHtml: the native module has no JS fallback in the Jest environment and the test suite crashes on import rather than failing a specific assertion.

lessonTitle: React Native: Testing with Jest, React Native Testing Library, and Maestro

bodyHtml: visual regression belongs to Storybook or a dedicated screenshot tool, not a component test's toHaveClass-style assertion.

lessonTitle: Electron: Process Model and Typed IPC Channels

lead: Validating the payload but not the sender

lessonTitle: Electron: Process Model and Typed IPC Channels

lessonTitle: Electron: Process Model and Typed IPC Channels

lessonTitle: Electron: Process Model and Typed IPC Channels
lead: Passing the raw `IpcRendererEvent` through to a renderer callback

lessonTitle: Electron: Process Model and Typed IPC Channels
lead: Forgetting to return the unsubscribe function from a wrapped listener

lessonTitle: Electron: Preload Scripts and Context Isolation

lessonTitle: Electron: Preload Scripts and Context Isolation

bodyHtml: (contextBridge.exposeInMainWorld("electron", { ipcRenderer, fs: require("fs") })) — hands the renderer the exact filesystem access the sandbox exists to prevent.

lessonTitle: Electron: Preload Scripts and Context Isolation

lessonTitle: Electron: Preload Scripts and Context Isolation
lead: Leaving `setWindowOpenHandler` unset or defaulting to `{ action: "allow" }`

lessonTitle: Electron: Preload Scripts and Context Isolation
lead: Re-declaring `window.api`'s shape by hand in the renderer instead of importing the preload's exported type

lessonTitle: Electron: Preload Scripts and Context Isolation

lessonTitle: Electron: Main Process Lifecycle and Window Management

lessonTitle: Electron: Main Process Lifecycle and Window Management
lead: Skipping `app.requestSingleInstanceLock()`

lessonTitle: Electron: Main Process Lifecycle and Window Management
lead: Scattering `new BrowserWindow(...)` calls across multiple files

lessonTitle: Electron: Main Process Lifecycle and Window Management
lead: Persisting window bounds to `localStorage`
bodyHtml: it's renderer-scoped and gone on the next launch; window state has to live in a main-side store.

lessonTitle: Electron: Main Process Lifecycle and Window Management
lead: Restoring saved bounds without checking connected displays

lessonTitle: Electron: Main Process Lifecycle and Window Management

lessonTitle: Electron: Project Structure and electron-vite Build Configuration

lessonTitle: Electron: Project Structure and electron-vite Build Configuration

lessonTitle: Electron: Project Structure and electron-vite Build Configuration

lessonTitle: Electron: Project Structure and electron-vite Build Configuration

bodyHtml: either breaks HMR in development or risks a production build accidentally pointing at a dev server address.

lessonTitle: Electron: Project Structure and electron-vite Build Configuration
