lead: Too large a blast radius
bodyHtml: do not kill your entire database cluster for a first experiment. Kill one read replica, or inject 10% errors on one service, and observe from there.

lessonTitle: Chaos Engineering Fundamentals — Failure Injection
lead: Chaos without observability
bodyHtml: chaos experiments are useless if you cannot see what is happening. Set up logging, metrics, and traces before running chaos; otherwise you are flying blind.

lessonTitle: Infrastructure as Code — Terraform / Pulumi
lead: Storing the state file with secrets unencrypted, or committing it to git
bodyHtml: it often contains sensitive values in plaintext

lessonTitle: Cloud Architecture & Well-Architected Patterns — Multi-Region, FinOps
lead: Going multi-region "because it sounds robust" without a tested failover
bodyHtml: an untested DR plan is not a DR plan

lessonTitle: Contributing to Popular Open Source Projects
lead: Opening a large PR without prior discussion
bodyHtml: A 500-line feature PR with no prior issue discussion will almost always be rejected or ignored — maintainers do not accept large changes without architectural discussion first; open an issue proposing the change and wait for feedback before writing code

lessonTitle: Contributing to Popular Open Source Projects
lead: Skipping the existing test suite
bodyHtml: If your change breaks existing tests, your PR will not be merged; always run the full test suite before opening the PR, even if you are only changing documentation

lessonTitle: Contributing to Popular Open Source Projects
lead: Duplicating an existing open PR
bodyHtml: Before starting work, search both issues and PRs for your topic; opening a duplicate wastes your time and the maintainer's time; if a stale PR exists, offer to take it over

lessonTitle: Contributing to Popular Open Source Projects
lead: Taking negative feedback personally
bodyHtml: Maintainers sometimes decline contributions that represent real improvements due to constraints you cannot see (roadmap conflicts, pending rewrites, performance concerns); "we're not taking this direction right now" is not a judgment of your skill

lessonTitle: Publishing and Maintaining Your Own Open Source Tool
lead: Building a framework instead of a tool
bodyHtml: A framework requires users to structure their application around it; a tool has a clear input and output and fits into any structure; start with a tool — frameworks require adoption at a level that takes years

lessonTitle: Publishing and Maintaining Your Own Open Source Tool
lead: Publishing without a README
bodyHtml: A package with no documentation gets no adoption; write the README before the code (README-driven development is legitimate) so you are clear on the interface before you implement it

lessonTitle: Publishing and Maintaining Your Own Open Source Tool
lead: Not setting expectations about maintenance
bodyHtml: A repository with open issues and no response for 6 months looks abandoned even if you check in occasionally; add an explicit maintenance badge (maintained: yes/limited/no) and close issues that are out of scope

lessonTitle: Publishing and Maintaining Your Own Open Source Tool
lead: Scope expansion under community pressure
bodyHtml: When your small, well-focused tool starts getting stars, community members will open issues requesting features that expand the scope; it is healthy to say "that is out of scope for this package — here is why" in the issue

lessonTitle: Semver and Changelog Management
lead: Using git tags as a changelog substitute
bodyHtml: git log v1.0.0..v1.1.0 --oneline is not a changelog; it contains implementation details written for developers, not adoption decisions written for consumers

lessonTitle: Semver and Changelog Management
lead: MAJOR version fear
bodyHtml: Some developers increment MINOR for breaking changes to avoid the scary 2.0.0 number; this breaks the semver contract — downstream consumers who trust semver will have silent breakage; increment MAJOR without hesitation for breaking changes

lessonTitle: Semver and Changelog Management
lead: Inconsistent commit messages that prevent automation
bodyHtml: If you adopt Conventional Commits, enforce them with a commit-msg hook (commitlint) from day one; a mix of conventional and non-conventional messages makes automated changelog generation produce incomplete output

lessonTitle: Semver and Changelog Management
lead: Not documenting the migration path for breaking changes
bodyHtml: A CHANGELOG entry that says "removed X" without explaining what to use instead or how to migrate is worse than no changelog — it tells users something broke without helping them fix it

lessonTitle: Publishing npm / GitHub Packages
lead: Publishing `src/` instead of `dist/`
bodyHtml: The files field in package.json determines what is published; if you omit it, the entire repository is published including source, tests, and node_modules — use "files": ["dist"] always

lessonTitle: Publishing npm / GitHub Packages
lead: Not building before publishing
bodyHtml: Forgetting to rebuild after the last code change means you publish stale compiled output; the prepublishOnly script that runs build prevents this

lessonTitle: Publishing npm / GitHub Packages
lead: Publishing with a personal access token in CI
bodyHtml: Personal tokens have the permissions of your entire account; use an automation-type npm token scoped to the specific package for CI; rotate it when a workflow file changes

lessonTitle: Conference / Meetup Speaking
lead: Submitting to major conferences before speaking at meetups
bodyHtml: A JSConf CFP with no speaking history has a single-digit acceptance rate; a local TypeScript meetup CFP with no history has a > 50% acceptance rate; build the track record first

lessonTitle: Conference / Meetup Speaking
lead: Making the abstract too broad
bodyHtml: "I'll talk about multi-tenant SaaS" is a topic, not a proposal; "I'll show how to enforce tenant isolation at the TypeORM data source layer with code examples" is a talk — specificity is what gets accepted

lessonTitle: Conference / Meetup Speaking
lead: Not rehearsing out loud
bodyHtml: Reading slides silently is not rehearsal; you must rehearse speaking at full speed to discover which transitions are awkward, which code examples need simplification, and whether you are within the time limit

lessonTitle: Conference / Meetup Speaking
lead: No clear takeaway
bodyHtml: A talk that ends with "and that's my experience building SaaS" gives the audience nothing to act on; define the one thing you want every attendee to do differently starting tomorrow and state it explicitly in the closing

lessonTitle: Risk-Based Security Scoping & Threat Model Lite
lead: Skipping the "residual risk" column entirely
bodyHtml: every control has limits, and not naming what's left over gives false confidence

lessonTitle: Third-Party Vendor Risk & Data Processing Agreements
lead: Treating "the provider has a DPA available" as equivalent to "the DPA is reviewed and signed"
bodyHtml: availability is not adoption

lessonTitle: Children's Data Compliance — Age Verification & Parental Consent
lead: "We don't market to children" is the whole compliance argument for the UK Children's Code
bodyHtml: Assuming "we don't market to children" satisfies the UK Children's Code, which tests accessibility, not marketing intent

lessonTitle: Children's Data Compliance — Age Verification & Parental Consent
lead: A COPPA-scoped service uses a friendly, game-like age-verification screen
bodyHtml: Using a friendly, game-like age-verification screen for a COPPA-scoped service, when a neutral screen is specifically required

lessonTitle: Children's Data Compliance — Age Verification & Parental Consent
lead: An under-13 user hits the age gate and is simply blocked, no path forward
bodyHtml: Treating an under-13 (or under-16, depending on jurisdiction) user as simply blocked, instead of routed to a real, working parental-consent mechanism

lessonTitle: Children's Data Compliance — Age Verification & Parental Consent
lead: Age verification asks for a full ID scan or exact birthdate
bodyHtml: Collecting a full ID scan or exact birthdate to verify age when a simple, proportionate self-declared age check would have sufficed — over-collecting to solve a minimization problem

lessonTitle: Children's Data Compliance — Age Verification & Parental Consent
lead: The same age threshold (always 13) applies to every visitor regardless of where they're located
bodyHtml: Applying a single global age threshold (e.g., always 13) across all users instead of routing by the visitor's jurisdiction, which produces under-compliance in the EU/UK and over-collection in the US

lessonTitle: Health Data Compliance — HIPAA, NHS & KVKK Sağlık Verileri
lead: Accepting "it's just a patient portal" as a reason to skip HIPAA/KVKK/NHS scoping, when the use case
bodyHtml: not the client's framing — determines applicability

lessonTitle: Security Handover & Access Transition Checklist
lead: The engagement ends, and production hosting is still under your personal login
bodyHtml: Leaving production hosting, domain, or vendor accounts under a freelancer's personal login after the engagement ends, with no transfer plan

lessonTitle: Security Handover & Access Transition Checklist
lead: Credentials get sent over in a plain chat message
bodyHtml: Sending credentials in a plain document or chat message instead of a secure transfer channel or the client's password manager

lessonTitle: Security Handover & Access Transition Checklist
lead: The handover doc doesn't mention that no pentest or restore test was ever run
bodyHtml: Omitting a known limitation (no pentest, no restore test) from the handover to make the delivery look more complete than it is

lessonTitle: Security Handover & Access Transition Checklist
lead: A former team member's access is still active weeks after they left the project
bodyHtml: Leaving a contractor's or former team member's access active because no one performed the access review at the point they left

lessonTitle: Security Handover & Access Transition Checklist
lead: A handover conversation ends with "I'll keep an eye on it," no maintenance contract behind that
bodyHtml: Implying ongoing security support ("I'll keep an eye on it") without a contracted maintenance agreement backing that statement — an informal promise nobody is actually resourced to keep

lessonTitle: Client-Facing Security Communication — Risk Framing & Scope Boundaries
lead: Discussing an active incident publicly or with end users without the client's approval, when the client
bodyHtml: not the development team — usually owns that external communication decision

lessonTitle: Writing ADRs (Architecture Decision Records)
lead: ADRs without real negatives
bodyHtml: if every consequence is positive and there are no trade-offs documented, the ADR is marketing, not engineering. Every real decision has costs; document them.

lessonTitle: Writing ADRs (Architecture Decision Records)
lead: Options section with only the chosen option
bodyHtml: the value of an ADR is the rejected alternatives. If you only document what you chose, a future maintainer cannot evaluate whether the constraints have changed.

lessonTitle: Writing ADRs (Architecture Decision Records)
lead: Updating an ADR when a decision changes
bodyHtml: never edit an accepted ADR's Decision section. Write a new ADR, mark it Superseded, and link both. The history of the decision is as valuable as the current decision.

lessonTitle: Writing ADRs (Architecture Decision Records)
lead: One massive ADR per component
bodyHtml: one ADR per decision, not per component. A database ADR, a caching ADR, a session strategy ADR, and a migration strategy ADR are four separate records, not one "data layer" ADR.

lessonTitle: RFC (Request for Comments) Process Management
lead: Writing the RFC after the decision is already made
bodyHtml: This turns the RFC into theater, not thinking — it eliminates the ability to course-correct based on feedback

lessonTitle: RFC (Request for Comments) Process Management
lead: Making the RFC too long before opening it for comments
bodyHtml: A three-page draft that invites comments is more useful than a ten-page document that discourages them; write enough to be concrete, then share early

lessonTitle: RFC (Request for Comments) Process Management
lead: No explicit rejection of alternatives
bodyHtml: Future collaborators (including yourself) will re-propose the same rejected alternatives if you do not document why they were discarded

lessonTitle: RFC (Request for Comments) Process Management
lead: No lifecycle tracking
bodyHtml: RFCs that are accepted but never marked "superseded" when things change become a source of confusion — keep the status field current

lessonTitle: Technical Debt Prioritization — Risk × Cost Matrix
lead: Gut-feel prioritization without scoring
bodyHtml: "I feel like the auth module needs refactoring" is not comparable to "I feel like the billing module needs refactoring" — scores make tradeoffs explicit and auditable

lessonTitle: Technical Debt Prioritization — Risk × Cost Matrix
lead: Letting the register go stale
bodyHtml: A debt register that hasn't been updated in three months is worse than no register because it creates false confidence; review and re-score quarterly

lessonTitle: Technical Debt Prioritization — Risk × Cost Matrix
lead: Ignoring interest rate
bodyHtml: Isolated high-risk debt is less urgent than medium-risk debt that touches every feature — failing to account for interest rate leads to consistently wrong ordering

lessonTitle: Technical Debt Prioritization — Risk × Cost Matrix
lead: Treating all debt as bad
bodyHtml: Some debt is a deliberate, time-boxed tradeoff made to hit a deadline — mark these explicitly with a scheduled payback date, not as permanent items

lessonTitle: Code Review Culture — Critique Code, Not People
lead: No explicit blocker vs. suggestion distinction
bodyHtml: Authors waste time addressing nit comments they thought were required, or ignore blocker comments they thought were optional

lessonTitle: Code Review Culture — Critique Code, Not People
lead: Reviewing the implementation, not the intent
bodyHtml: Jumping straight to "I would have done this differently" without first confirming you understood what the PR is trying to accomplish leads to irrelevant feedback

lessonTitle: Code Review Culture — Critique Code, Not People
lead: Approving to avoid conflict
bodyHtml: "Looks good to me" on a PR you did not read is worse than not reviewing — it signals that the review process has no real function

lessonTitle: Code Review Culture — Critique Code, Not People
lead: Making the review about the reviewer
bodyHtml: "I never write it this way" is not a valid review comment unless "this way" is demonstrably incorrect or violates a documented standard

lessonTitle: Blameless Post-Mortem — Writing and Running One
lead: Writing it more than 48 hours after resolution
bodyHtml: Memory degrades fast, especially for the exact timeline; the draft needs to be written while the incident is still fresh

lessonTitle: Blameless Post-Mortem — Writing and Running One
lead: Action items without owners or dates
bodyHtml: "We should add more monitoring" is not an action item; "Add latency alert for /api/payment/webhook endpoint by 2025-06-15 — owner: me" is

lessonTitle: Blameless Post-Mortem — Writing and Running One
lead: Treating the first "why" as the root cause
bodyHtml: A deploy caused an outage — but why did the deploy reach production without catching this? Why was there no circuit breaker? Five whys often takes you to a process or tooling gap, not a code bug

lessonTitle: Blameless Post-Mortem — Writing and Running One
lead: Never reading past post-mortems
bodyHtml: The entire value of writing post-mortems is destroyed if you never reference them; review them before major deploys and quarterly for pattern analysis

lessonTitle: Mentorship — Pair Programming Structure, Junior Guidance
lead: Taking over the keyboard
bodyHtml: The moment you take over, the mentee stops thinking and starts watching — every takeover is a missed learning opportunity; if you must show something, narrate every keystroke

lessonTitle: Mentorship — Pair Programming Structure, Junior Guidance
lead: Mentoring on output, not thinking
bodyHtml: "Here's the correct code" teaches the answer; "What question should we ask before writing any code?" teaches the process; only one of these scales

lessonTitle: Mentorship — Pair Programming Structure, Junior Guidance
lead: No follow-up task
bodyHtml: A pairing session without a concrete independent task to complete before the next session means you will redo the same teaching next session — the follow-up task is what converts pairing into retained skill

lessonTitle: Mentorship — Pair Programming Structure, Junior Guidance
lead: Confusing mentorship with management
bodyHtml: Mentorship is about the mentee's growth; management is about task completion — mixing the two creates sessions where you're really just supervising work, not teaching, and the mentee makes no lasting progress

lessonTitle: Explaining Technical Concepts to Non-Technical Stakeholders
lead: Using jargon that sounds like plain English but isn't
bodyHtml: "We need to refactor the API to handle asynchronous webhook events" sounds clear to you and opaque to a client; never assume they know "API," "asynchronous," or "webhook" means the same thing you do

lessonTitle: Explaining Technical Concepts to Non-Technical Stakeholders
lead: Explaining the solution before establishing the problem
bodyHtml: A client who does not first understand why the database needs an index will never understand why it is worth 4 hours of work — always establish the "why it matters" before the "how we fix it"

lessonTitle: Explaining Technical Concepts to Non-Technical Stakeholders
lead: Treating every technical question as an invitation to teach
bodyHtml: Sometimes the client asking "how does the database work?" is really asking "is my data safe?" — answer the underlying question, not the surface one

lessonTitle: Explaining Technical Concepts to Non-Technical Stakeholders
lead: Written explanations without structure
bodyHtml: Long paragraphs in an email are not read; use bold headers, bullet points, and short paragraphs; clients skim, not read

lessonTitle: Estimation — Confidence Intervals Instead of Story Points
lead: Single-point estimates to clients
bodyHtml: "Five days" sounds confident; "four to seven days with five being most likely" sounds honest — the second builds more long-term trust because it proves accurate over time

lessonTitle: Estimation — Confidence Intervals Instead of Story Points
lead: Not decomposing before estimating
bodyHtml: A "build the dashboard" estimate is useless; "implement five chart components, wire up three API endpoints, and write unit tests" is estimable — decompose to tasks of 2–8 hours before estimating

lessonTitle: Estimation — Confidence Intervals Instead of Story Points
lead: Optimism bias unchecked
bodyHtml: Most developers' "optimistic" estimates are actually their "everything goes perfectly, I have no meetings, no bugs, and unlimited focus" estimates — these never occur; pad your optimistic estimate by 20% to account for baseline friction

lessonTitle: Estimation — Confidence Intervals Instead of Story Points
lead: Not tracking calibration
bodyHtml: Estimation improves only through feedback; if you never compare your estimates to actuals, your confidence intervals are just theater — log every estimate and review monthly

lessonTitle: Scope Creep Management — Saying No with Alternatives
lead: Starting work before written approval
bodyHtml: Verbal agreement on a CR is not a CR — a client who approved verbally and then disputes the cost will point to the lack of written record; never start CR work without written confirmation

lessonTitle: Scope Creep Management — Saying No with Alternatives
lead: Issuing a CR without options
bodyHtml: "This is out of scope, it will cost $X" is a wall; "here are your three options and my recommendation" is a service — clients approve CRs faster when they feel they have agency

lessonTitle: Scope Creep Management — Saying No with Alternatives
lead: Not distinguishing bug from CR
bodyHtml: If you deliver something that does not meet the specification, that is a bug and you fix it at your cost; if the client wants something different from the specification, that is a CR and they pay for it — conflating these is expensive

lessonTitle: Scope Creep Management — Saying No with Alternatives
lead: Absorbing without documenting
bodyHtml: If you absorb a change, send an email noting that you are including it as a courtesy and that future similar additions will go through the formal CR process — undocumented absorptions create an expectation that all small additions are free

lessonTitle: Technical Interview Design — Asking and Evaluating
lead: Testing trivia instead of judgment
bodyHtml: "What does typeof null === 'object' return?" tests memorization; "here is a function that uses typeof to check types — is there a bug?" tests the same knowledge through applied reasoning, which is what you need on the job

lessonTitle: Technical Interview Design — Asking and Evaluating
lead: No rubric, pure intuition
bodyHtml: Without a rubric, interviewers consistently prefer candidates who are similar to themselves (affinity bias), confident talkers over careful thinkers, and people who use familiar frameworks; a rubric does not eliminate bias but it constrains it

lessonTitle: Technical Interview Design — Asking and Evaluating
lead: Live coding under pressure as the primary signal
bodyHtml: Some developers perform very poorly in live coding under observation but perform very well given a reasonable time window; a take-home with a live walkthrough gives you signal about the work without filtering for stress-tolerance specifically

lessonTitle: Technical Interview Design — Asking and Evaluating
lead: Not giving candidates time to ask questions
bodyHtml: A candidate who asks sharp, specific questions about your architecture or workflow is demonstrating curiosity and due diligence; a candidate who has no questions either did no research or has no standards — both are signal

lessonTitle: Product Strategy Operating System — From Problem to Roadmap
lead: Skipping the risk and assumption log because the project "feels simple"
bodyHtml: simple projects still have unvalidated assumptions, they just have fewer of them

lessonTitle: Problem Framing — Converting Vague Requests into Problem Statements
lead: Inventing pain points because the real ones weren't investigated
bodyHtml: a fabricated problem statement is more dangerous than an honest "unknown," because it looks resolved

lessonTitle: Personas & Role Mapping — Buyer, User, Admin, and Operator
lead: Assuming the buyer and the user are the same person by default, without checking
bodyHtml: even solo internal tools often have a manager who approves and a staff member who executes

lessonTitle: Scope Boundaries — In Scope, Out of Scope, and Change Triggers
lead: Confusing "out of scope" with "rejected"
bodyHtml: out-of-scope items still belong on the roadmap, just not in this phase

lessonTitle: Feedback and Validation Loops — Testing Assumptions Before and After Launch
lead: Confusing a stakeholder's confidence in an assumption with evidence that it's true
bodyHtml: the whole point of validation is that confidence isn't proof

lessonTitle: Market and Competitive Positioning — Build, Buy, or Differentiate
lead: Skipping this gate for smaller projects, which often produces the most bloated MVPs
bodyHtml: a small client asking for "something like X" absorbs the incumbent's entire feature shape by default if nobody reframes the request

lessonTitle: Product Risk and Assumption Log
lead: The risk log lives in scattered chat messages and meeting notes, not one shared document
bodyHtml: Keeping the log informally in chat history or meeting notes instead of a structured, shared document with owners and statuses

lessonTitle: Product Risk and Assumption Log
lead: A risk got logged once, months ago, status still "Open"
bodyHtml: Recording a risk once and never revisiting its status, so "Open" risks silently become "ignored" risks

lessonTitle: Product Risk and Assumption Log
lead: A high-severity risk is still unaddressed, and the proposal is about to be signed
bodyHtml: Letting a high-severity risk ride into a signed proposal because addressing it felt like it would slow down the sale

lessonTitle: Product Risk and Assumption Log
lead: An unresolved unknown gets a shrug and "we'll figure it out later"
bodyHtml: Saying "we'll figure it out later" instead of the professional reframe: naming the assumption explicitly and tying it to a validation step before pricing is locked

lessonTitle: Product Risk and Assumption Log
lead: The risk log only ever gets opened by the PM
bodyHtml: Treating the log as the PM's private tracking tool rather than a document the client and delivery team both see and act on

lessonTitle: Release Strategy — Alpha, Beta, Pilot, and Rollout
lead: Choosing a rollout strategy that doesn't match the pilot context
bodyHtml: for example, a single-launch release when the pilot context specifically named one region as the controlled first exposure

lessonTitle: Technical Architecture Operating System, Principles, and Decision Gates
lead: Writing an ADR for a trivial implementation detail while skipping one for a decision
bodyHtml: like the monolith-vs-service-split call — that actually locks in future migration cost

lessonTitle: Requirements-to-Architecture Translation and System Context Mapping
lead: Database tables and API routes get designed straight from a one-sentence pitch
bodyHtml: Designing database tables or API routes directly from a one-sentence product pitch, skipping the translation step entirely

lessonTitle: Requirements-to-Architecture Translation and System Context Mapping
lead: A third-party integration has no fallback for what happens when that system is down
bodyHtml: Assuming a third-party system is always available and building no fallback behavior for the case where it isn't

lessonTitle: Requirements-to-Architecture Translation and System Context Mapping
lead: "The client will provide clean data" is treated as a given, never written down as an assumption
bodyHtml: Treating "the client will provide clean data" as a certainty instead of stating it explicitly as an assumption with a named risk

lessonTitle: Requirements-to-Architecture Translation and System Context Mapping
lead: The system context map gets drawn after implementation has already started
bodyHtml: Drawing the system context map after implementation has already started, once boundary decisions are already baked into the code

lessonTitle: Requirements-to-Architecture Translation and System Context Mapping
lead: Public, authenticated, and privileged boundaries all get the same validation logic
bodyHtml: Applying uniform trust and validation logic across all boundaries instead of treating public, authenticated, and privileged boundaries differently

lessonTitle: Domain Modeling, Module Boundaries, and the Staged Scaling Path
lead: Treating a service split as reversible and low-cost when it is neither
bodyHtml: extracting a service is a one-way door that should require a documented ADR (lesson 387)

lessonTitle: Technology Selection and New-Technology Governance
lead: Treating technology selection and vendor evaluation as the same decision
bodyHtml: a stack choice and a specific vendor's contract terms are different questions with different owners

lessonTitle: Non-Functional Requirements and Production Readiness Strategy
lead: A requirements doc says the system must be "scalable" and "highly available," no numbers attached
bodyHtml: Saying "scalable," "secure," or "highly available" without defining what scale, which threats, or what uptime number is actually meant

lessonTitle: Non-Functional Requirements and Production Readiness Strategy
lead: The design covers the happy path; failure modes never got their own analysis pass
bodyHtml: Designing only for the happy path and treating failure-mode analysis as optional because "it probably won't happen"

lessonTitle: Non-Functional Requirements and Production Readiness Strategy
lead: The analytics service goes down, and checkout goes down with it
bodyHtml: Letting a non-critical dependency (analytics, a recommendation engine) block a critical user flow like checkout when it fails

lessonTitle: Non-Functional Requirements and Production Readiness Strategy
lead: Backups are assumed to be handled by the hosting platform, with no one having actually tested a restore
bodyHtml: Leaving backup and restore as an assumed platform feature instead of a stated, tested policy with an owner

lessonTitle: Non-Functional Requirements and Production Readiness Strategy
lead: Serverless or VPS gets picked because it's the one you know, not because it matches the traffic pattern
bodyHtml: Deciding on serverless or VPS hosting by habit or familiarity rather than by matching the project's actual traffic pattern and operational capacity

lessonTitle: Data Architecture — Ownership, Source of Truth, and Lifecycle Strategy
lead: Tables get created before the team agrees on what the domain terms actually mean
bodyHtml: Creating database tables before domain terms and ownership are clear, producing schema that encodes technical convenience instead of business meaning

lessonTitle: Data Architecture — Ownership, Source of Truth, and Lifecycle Strategy
lead: Full card data gets stored in your own database instead of left with the payment provider
bodyHtml: Storing payment secrets or full card data locally instead of relying on the payment provider as the source of truth for that data

lessonTitle: Data Architecture — Ownership, Source of Truth, and Lifecycle Strategy
lead: A business-critical record gets hard-deleted because that's the simplest code path
bodyHtml: Hard-deleting business-critical records by default because it's the simplest code path, without considering audit or reporting consequences

lessonTitle: Data Architecture — Ownership, Source of Truth, and Lifecycle Strategy
lead: The same customer record is owned and edited in two different systems with no sync strategy between them
bodyHtml: Duplicating a data object's ownership across two systems with no defined sync strategy, so the two systems drift out of agreement silently

lessonTitle: Data Architecture — Ownership, Source of Truth, and Lifecycle Strategy
lead: An index gets added because it seems like it might help someday
bodyHtml: Adding indexes speculatively instead of deriving them from actual identified query patterns

lessonTitle: API, Integration, and Event-Driven Architecture Decisions
lead: Skipping the exit strategy field because switching providers feels hypothetical
bodyHtml: until pricing changes or the provider shuts down and there's no abstraction in place

lessonTitle: Auth, Identity, and Multi-Tenancy Architecture Decisions
lead: SSO gets added because it looks professional, with no client requirement actually asking for it
bodyHtml: Adding SSO or social login because it looks professional, without a client requirement actually calling for it, adding implementation cost with no corresponding need

lessonTitle: Auth, Identity, and Multi-Tenancy Architecture Decisions
lead: A `tenantId` column gets added "just in case," with no membership model or role scoping behind it
bodyHtml: Adding a tenantId column "just in case" without the accompanying membership model, role scoping, and audit strategy that make tenant isolation actually work

lessonTitle: Auth, Identity, and Multi-Tenancy Architecture Decisions
lead: Tenant data separation happens by filtering in the frontend, not enforced on the server
bodyHtml: Relying on frontend-only filtering to separate tenant data instead of enforcing tenant scope server-side on every query

lessonTitle: Auth, Identity, and Multi-Tenancy Architecture Decisions
lead: Per-tenant database isolation gets built before it's confirmed the product will ever have more than one tenant
bodyHtml: Building enterprise-grade per-tenant database isolation before validating that the product needs more than one tenant at all

lessonTitle: Auth, Identity, and Multi-Tenancy Architecture Decisions
lead: Cross-jurisdiction compliance gets raised as a legal question after the isolation model is already built
bodyHtml: Treating cross-jurisdiction compliance as a legal afterthought instead of an architecture constraint that determines the isolation model upfront

lessonTitle: Legacy System Assessment and Migration Strategy
lead: A clean migration gets promised before anyone has actually looked at a real data sample
bodyHtml: Promising a clean migration before seeing an actual sample of the real data, then discovering format inconsistencies mid-execution

lessonTitle: Legacy System Assessment and Migration Strategy
lead: Every historical record gets migrated by default, no one asked what can just be archived
bodyHtml: Migrating every historical record by default instead of asking which ones the business actually needs versus can archive

lessonTitle: Legacy System Assessment and Migration Strategy
lead: A destructive migration step runs with no pre-migration backup, because it "should just work"
bodyHtml: Skipping a pre-migration backup before a destructive operation because the migration "should just work"

lessonTitle: Legacy System Assessment and Migration Strategy
lead: Cutover happens as an informal step, no defined go/no-go moment or rollback condition
bodyHtml: Treating the cutover as an informal step instead of a planned event with a defined go/no-go decision and rollback condition

lessonTitle: Legacy System Assessment and Migration Strategy
lead: The system cuts over to the new version with no explicit client sign-off on record
bodyHtml: Cutting over without explicit client sign-off, leaving ambiguity later about whether the client actually approved the final migrated state

lessonTitle: SaaS Metrics — MRR, Churn, LTV, CAC
lead: Using gross revenue instead of MRR
bodyHtml: Annual subscriptions paid upfront inflate apparent revenue; always normalize to monthly to compare periods fairly

lessonTitle: SaaS Metrics — MRR, Churn, LTV, CAC
lead: Customer churn vs. revenue churn
bodyHtml: Losing a $10/month customer and a $200/month customer both count as "1 churned customer" in customer churn rate — revenue churn rate weights them correctly and matters more

lessonTitle: SaaS Metrics — MRR, Churn, LTV, CAC
lead: Ignoring free trial conversion as a metric
bodyHtml: If your boilerplate includes trial days, trial-to-paid conversion rate is a leading indicator of future MRR that most operators track too late

lessonTitle: SaaS Metrics — MRR, Churn, LTV, CAC
lead: LTV without gross margin
bodyHtml: LTV calculated on revenue, not gross profit, overstates true customer value; subtract hosting, payment processing, and support costs from MRR before calculating LTV

lessonTitle: Payment Integration Depth — Webhook Idempotency, Dispute Handling
lead: Using `request.json()` for webhook body
bodyHtml: Stripe signature verification requires the raw request body; using request.json() parses it first and the bytes do not match the signature — always use request.text() or request.arrayBuffer()

lessonTitle: Payment Integration Depth — Webhook Idempotency, Dispute Handling
lead: Returning 4xx for unhandled event types
bodyHtml: Returning 4xx tells Stripe the webhook failed and triggers retries; return 200 for unhandled event types and log them — only return 500 when you want a retry

lessonTitle: Payment Integration Depth — Webhook Idempotency, Dispute Handling
lead: Idempotency at the application level only (not database)
bodyHtml: Race conditions between concurrent webhook deliveries can bypass application-level checks; the unique constraint at the database level is the only reliable guard

lessonTitle: Payment Integration Depth — Webhook Idempotency, Dispute Handling
lead: Waiting to collect dispute evidence
bodyHtml: The dispute window (7–21 days) feels long but Stripe requires evidence before the deadline; automate evidence collection on charge.dispute.created so the evidence is always ready when you need to submit

lessonTitle: Email Deliverability — SPF, DKIM, DMARC, Bounce Management
lead: Using the root domain for transactional email
bodyHtml: If transactional email reputation suffers (one bad campaign), it can affect deliverability for human-sent emails from the same domain; use a subdomain (notifications.yourdomain.com) to isolate reputation

lessonTitle: Email Deliverability — SPF, DKIM, DMARC, Bounce Management
lead: Setting DMARC to `p=reject` on day one
bodyHtml: If your SPF or DKIM is misconfigured (common), p=reject means legitimate emails are silently dropped; start with p=none and promote to quarantine and reject only after validating reports

lessonTitle: Email Deliverability — SPF, DKIM, DMARC, Bounce Management
lead: Not processing bounce webhooks
bodyHtml: Your email provider suppresses bounced addresses in their system, but if your application retries a send (e.g., for a reminder email), you may be hitting hard-bounced addresses from your own logic — the suppression table in your own database is necessary

lessonTitle: Email Deliverability — SPF, DKIM, DMARC, Bounce Management
lead: Forgetting email authentication when switching providers
bodyHtml: Each provider has its own DKIM key; switching from SendGrid to Resend requires adding new DKIM DNS records before removing old ones — gaps in DKIM coverage cause deliverability drops

lessonTitle: Internationalization (i18n) — Timezone, Currency, RTL Support
lead: Storing dates in local timezone
bodyHtml: A subscription created at "midnight" for a user in Tokyo stored as local time becomes a different UTC day — every cross-timezone query is wrong; always store UTC, always

lessonTitle: Internationalization (i18n) — Timezone, Currency, RTL Support
lead: Rolling your own currency formatting
bodyHtml: "$" + (amount / 100).toFixed(2) is incorrect for non-USD currencies, produces wrong decimal separators in many locales, and fails for currencies without cents; use Intl.NumberFormat and never touch it again

lessonTitle: Internationalization (i18n) — Timezone, Currency, RTL Support
lead: Adding RTL as an afterthought
bodyHtml: Trying to mirror a layout built with physical CSS properties (left, right, float) after the fact requires touching every stylesheet rule; CSS logical properties cost nothing to use from the start and pay back when RTL support is needed

lessonTitle: Internationalization (i18n) — Timezone, Currency, RTL Support
lead: Single global locale
bodyHtml: In a multi-tenant SaaS, two tenants may use different languages, timezones, and currencies; locale must be a per-tenant (and optionally per-user) setting, not a single application-level configuration

lessonTitle: Accessibility (a11y) — WCAG 2.1 AA Compliance
lead: Using `<div>` and `<span>` for interactive elements
bodyHtml: A <div onClick> does not receive keyboard focus, does not fire on Enter/Space, and is announced as "blank" by screen readers; always use <button> for clickable actions and <a> for navigation

lessonTitle: Accessibility (a11y) — WCAG 2.1 AA Compliance
lead: Adding ARIA without keyboard support
bodyHtml: role="button" tells screen readers "this is a button" but does not make the element focusable or operable via keyboard; ARIA attributes do not add behavior, only semantics — pair every ARIA role with the corresponding keyboard interaction

lessonTitle: Accessibility (a11y) — WCAG 2.1 AA Compliance
lead: Skipping color contrast testing
bodyHtml: Designers often choose colors that look fine on a well-calibrated monitor but fail 4.5:1 contrast; run your color palette through a contrast checker during design, not after implementation

lessonTitle: Accessibility (a11y) — WCAG 2.1 AA Compliance
lead: Not managing focus in SPAs
bodyHtml: When a page changes in a Next.js application, the browser does not move focus to the new content — screen reader users hear nothing; use router.events or server component navigation callbacks to announce page changes and move focus to the main heading

lessonTitle: Mobile-First API Design — Bandwidth, Offline-First Thinking
lead: Using offset pagination for mobile
bodyHtml: page=2&limit=20 skips 20 records — if one new record was inserted before your first request, page 2 duplicates a record; cursor-based pagination is immune to this and more efficient for the database

lessonTitle: Mobile-First API Design — Bandwidth, Offline-First Thinking
lead: Returning full objects in list views
bodyHtml: An endpoint that powers a list of 50 tenants and returns 2KB per tenant sends 100KB; with sparse fieldsets requesting only id, name, and status, the same list is 5KB — a 20× bandwidth reduction

lessonTitle: Mobile-First API Design — Bandwidth, Offline-First Thinking
lead: No compression
bodyHtml: Next.js enables gzip by default in production, but if you are behind a custom proxy or running on edge runtimes, verify compression is active; 70–80% bandwidth reduction for JSON is essentially free performance

lessonTitle: Mobile-First API Design — Bandwidth, Offline-First Thinking
lead: Designing sync as "full re-download"
bodyHtml: A mobile app that fetches the full dataset every time it reconnects will be slow and drain battery; design delta sync endpoints from the start, even if the client does not use them immediately

lessonTitle: Analytics Integration — Event Design, Funnel Analysis
lead: Tracking UI actions instead of business actions
bodyHtml: button_clicked with no context is nearly useless; track what the button did (subscription_upgrade_initiated), not that it was clicked

lessonTitle: Analytics Integration — Event Design, Funnel Analysis
lead: Not tracking tenant identity (group calls)
bodyHtml: In a multi-tenant SaaS, user-level analytics are incomplete — if you only track users, you cannot answer "what do enterprise tenants do differently from solo tenants?" — group calls are mandatory

lessonTitle: Analytics Integration — Event Design, Funnel Analysis
lead: Adding analytics directly in components
bodyHtml: When you call posthog.capture() directly in 40 components, switching providers requires 40 changes; the service abstraction layer means one change point

lessonTitle: Analytics Integration — Event Design, Funnel Analysis
lead: No consent management
bodyHtml: In the EU, tracking users without explicit consent is a GDPR violation; gate all analytics.identify() and analytics.track() calls on a consent flag stored in localStorage or a cookie consent service

lessonTitle: A/B Test Infrastructure — Statistical Significance
lead: Stopping early when results look good
bodyHtml: The p-value fluctuates naturally during a test; if you stop as soon as p < 0.05, your false-positive rate is much higher than 5% — commit to the sample size target before starting

lessonTitle: A/B Test Infrastructure — Statistical Significance
lead: Testing too many variants simultaneously
bodyHtml: Each additional variant requires proportionally more traffic to reach significance; stick to A/B (one control, one variant) until you have high traffic; A/B/C/D tests require 3–4× the traffic

lessonTitle: A/B Test Infrastructure — Statistical Significance
lead: Choosing the wrong randomization unit
bodyHtml: If you randomize by session instead of by user/tenant, the same user might see different variants across sessions — contaminating the experiment and reducing statistical power

lessonTitle: A/B Test Infrastructure — Statistical Significance
lead: Not tracking the experiment exposure event
bodyHtml: If you only track conversions without tracking when users were exposed to the experiment, you cannot calculate the conversion rate — always fire an exposure event when the variant is shown, not just when the user converts

lessonTitle: OWASP Top 10 — Practical Application
lead: Treating OWASP as a one-time exercise
bodyHtml: New code introduces new risks; security review should be part of your PR template

lessonTitle: OWASP Top 10 — Practical Application
lead: Focusing only on A03 (Injection)
bodyHtml: SQL injection is well-understood and your ORM covers it; A01 (access control) is statistically the most common real-world finding

lessonTitle: OWASP Top 10 — Practical Application
lead: Verbose error messages in production
bodyHtml: Stack traces and internal identifiers in API error responses are an A05 misconfiguration; return generic messages to clients

lessonTitle: OWASP Top 10 — Practical Application
lead: Assuming HTTPS = cryptographic safety
bodyHtml: A02 also covers secrets in logs, unencrypted PII at rest, and weak JWT signing keys; HTTPS is just one layer

lessonTitle: SQL Injection Protection
lead: Using `$queryRawUnsafe` for convenience
bodyHtml: Prisma's $queryRaw tagged template is equally convenient and completely safe; there is almost never a reason to use Unsafe

lessonTitle: SQL Injection Protection
lead: Forgetting LIKE wildcards
bodyHtml: Your app allows user search input? % in the search term alters the pattern without being an injection vulnerability, but it is still unintended behavior

lessonTitle: SQL Injection Protection
lead: Dynamic ORDER BY without an allowlist
bodyHtml: ORDER BY ${req.query.sort} is injection even with an ORM; the parameterization only applies to values, not SQL keywords and identifiers

lessonTitle: SQL Injection Protection
lead: Trusting previously sanitized data
bodyHtml: Second-order injection: a value stored safely from input A is later used in a raw query for operation B without re-parameterization; trace every raw query's inputs to their source

lessonTitle: Mass Assignment Protection — DTO Whitelist
lead: Partial update with full DTO
bodyHtml: Using UserDto.partial() for a PATCH endpoint is correct, but if UserDto includes userRole, admins would be settable via PATCH. Create dedicated update DTOs that explicitly exclude sensitive fields

lessonTitle: Mass Assignment Protection — DTO Whitelist
lead: Validating at the route layer but not the service layer
bodyHtml: If your service is called from multiple places (API route, worker job, admin script), the service itself must validate, not just the route handler

lessonTitle: Mass Assignment Protection — DTO Whitelist
lead: TypeScript type assertions bypassing Zod
bodyHtml: const dto = body as RegisterDtoType skips runtime validation entirely; always call .parse() or .safeParse(), never cast

lessonTitle: Mass Assignment Protection — DTO Whitelist
lead: Forgetting nested objects
bodyHtml: If your DTO accepts a preferences: {} object and that object maps to a database column, the nested Zod schema must also be a strict whitelist

lessonTitle: Content Security Policy (CSP) Headers
lead: `'unsafe-inline'` in `script-src`
bodyHtml: This negates most of the protection CSP offers; use nonces or hashes instead, even if it requires more setup

lessonTitle: Content Security Policy (CSP) Headers
lead: Setting CSP in `next.config.ts` headers array
bodyHtml: This works for static responses but does not support nonces (which require a per-request value); use middleware for nonce-based CSP

lessonTitle: Content Security Policy (CSP) Headers
lead: Forgetting `connect-src` for your API domain
bodyHtml: Your frontend's fetch() calls to /api/... will be blocked by CSP if connect-src only has 'self' and your API is on a different subdomain

lessonTitle: Content Security Policy (CSP) Headers
lead: One policy for all routes
bodyHtml: Some pages (the admin panel, the marketing site) have different third-party script needs; consider per-route CSP via middleware path matching

lessonTitle: Dependency Audit Automation (npm audit, Snyk, Dependabot)
lead: `npm install` in CI instead of `npm ci`
bodyHtml: npm install can update the lockfile silently; npm ci enforces it and is reproducible

lessonTitle: Dependency Audit Automation (npm audit, Snyk, Dependabot)
lead: Ignoring moderate-severity findings indefinitely
bodyHtml: Most breaches involve CVEs that were "only" moderate at first; review and triage regularly

lessonTitle: Dependency Audit Automation (npm audit, Snyk, Dependabot)
lead: Not pinning exact versions for security-critical packages
bodyHtml: Use ~ or ^ conservatively for packages like jsonwebtoken and bcrypt; Dependabot handles the updates

lessonTitle: Dependency Audit Automation (npm audit, Snyk, Dependabot)
lead: Bulk-dismissing Dependabot PRs
bodyHtml: Each PR represents a real published patch; auto-merge patch updates after tests pass rather than closing them

lessonTitle: Secrets Management — Vault / SSM / KMS Instead of Env Files
lead: Committing `.env` to version control
bodyHtml: Even .env.example with real values is a security incident; use .env.example with placeholder values only

lessonTitle: Secrets Management — Vault / SSM / KMS Instead of Env Files
lead: Long-lived static secrets with no rotation policy
bodyHtml: Even with a secrets manager, secrets that never rotate are a liability; set a rotation schedule for DB passwords and JWT secrets

lessonTitle: Secrets Management — Vault / SSM / KMS Instead of Env Files
lead: Putting secrets in Docker image build args
bodyHtml: Build args are visible in the image layer history; inject secrets at runtime, not build time

lessonTitle: Secrets Management — Vault / SSM / KMS Instead of Env Files
lead: Over-engineering before you have the problem
bodyHtml: Vault's full feature set (dynamic secrets, leasing) has real operational overhead; start with SSM Parameter Store and graduate to Vault when the need justifies it

lessonTitle: Penetration Testing Process
lead: Pentesting production
bodyHtml: Always test on staging; a successful injection or privilege escalation in production affects real users and real data

lessonTitle: Penetration Testing Process
lead: Not having a written scope/rules of engagement
bodyHtml: Without a document signed by you authorizing the tester, a pentest is legally indistinguishable from unauthorized access; even self-testing should be documented

lessonTitle: Penetration Testing Process
lead: Treating a clean pentest as permanent security
bodyHtml: A clean pentest on today's codebase says nothing about tomorrow's; new features introduce new attack surface

lessonTitle: Penetration Testing Process
lead: Hiring the cheapest option
bodyHtml: Automated scanner results sold as a "pentest" do not find business logic flaws, authorization bypasses, or race conditions; the value is in the human tester's creativity

lessonTitle: RBAC vs ABAC
lead: Role explosion
bodyHtml: Creating ADMIN_WITH_BILLING, ADMIN_WITHOUT_BILLING, MANAGER_READ_ONLY etc.; a sign that ABAC attributes would be cleaner than more roles

lessonTitle: RBAC vs ABAC
lead: Bypassing the role check in "emergency" situations
bodyHtml: Commented-out authorization guards accumulate and become permanent security gaps

lessonTitle: RBAC vs ABAC
lead: Checking roles in the UI only
bodyHtml: The UI might hide the "Delete" button for non-OWNERs, but if the API route does not also check, a direct API call bypasses it; enforce at the service/route layer, not only in the UI

lessonTitle: RBAC vs ABAC
lead: System admin can access all tenant data without tenant role
bodyHtml: Your design already handles this correctly (system ADMIN bypasses tenant membership check), but it means system admin accounts are high-value targets that deserve extra protection (MFA, impersonation audit log)

lessonTitle: Supply Chain Security — Lockfile, Package Integrity
lead: Not committing `package-lock.json`
bodyHtml: Some teams add it to .gitignore; this means CI installs different versions on every run and there is no integrity guarantee

lessonTitle: Supply Chain Security — Lockfile, Package Integrity
lead: Using `npm install` in CI
bodyHtml: This can silently update packages within the semver range, bypassing the lockfile's integrity guarantees; always use npm ci

lessonTitle: Supply Chain Security — Lockfile, Package Integrity
lead: Ignoring the `integrity` hash in PRs
bodyHtml: When a PR updates package-lock.json, the changed integrity fields are the actual security-relevant change; review them, not just the version number

lessonTitle: Supply Chain Security — Lockfile, Package Integrity
lead: Publishing your own packages without 2FA
bodyHtml: If you maintain any npm packages, enable 2FA on your npm account; a compromised npm account is a supply chain attack against your own users

lessonTitle: Compliance Frameworks — SOC 2, ISO 27001, HIPAA
lead: Confusing "compliant" with "secure"
bodyHtml: they overlap substantially but a passed audit doesn't guarantee an absence of vulnerabilities, and vice versa
